![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/ff93274daa7f179f86343e59b7cf277c0e70555fdfdd3cce113c3cba149b08ac.png)

An airplane $A$ is flying horizontally at a constant height of $800\,\text{m}$ above the ground. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the airplane and a nearby radar station $R$ is decreasing at a rate of $0.05$ radians per second. What is the speed of the aircraft as a function of $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/29d06d071e6983d3487426b08d5a5548a611134dcf116674d199f6d3de03f246.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the airplane's altitude, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the radar station and the airplane. The quantity $y=800$ meters does not change with time because the airplane stays at a constant altitude.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{800}{x} \\ x & =800\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(800\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-800{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-0.05$ (negative because the angle is decreasing). Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-800{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-800{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )(-0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the aircraft is $40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\,\text{m/s}.$

A boy $B$ is flying a kite $K$ with a $20\,\text{m}$ length of string. If the kite is rising vertically at a constant speed of $1\,\text{m/s},$ at what rate is the angle of elevation $\theta $ increasing when $\theta ={45}^{∘}?$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/236144ff93bd22f5c4460c31e20216c45d6f8ac85dc945321dadecc093f379e0.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the kite's height, and $z$ is the distance between the boy and the kite. The quantity $z=20$ meters does not change with time because the string's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{20} \\ y & =20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Converting the given information from degrees to radians, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $\theta ={45}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{180}^{∘}}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{1}{20} & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{20}$ radians per second.

A drone $D$ takes off from a point $P$ and climbs with an angle of elevation of ${60}^{∘}$ and a vertical speed of $4\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$ Assuming the angle of elevation doesn't change, calculate the actual speed of the drone in the direction it is traveling.
Round your answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/69314419f6e0b93236fc048c6b9b6b262b09ff2cc061996353fbe23870a12726.png)

Let $y$ denote the vertical distance from the drone's projection to the starting point, and $z$ be the distance between the drone and the starting point, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={60}^{∘},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ z & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=4\text{km}/\text{h}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot 4≈4.62
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the speed of the drone is approximately $4.62\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

Ethan notices a drone descending. He estimates that the distance between his location and the point on the ground directly beneath the drone is $150\,\text{ft}.$ If the angle of elevation $\theta $ between him and the drone decreases at a rate of $0.1\,\text{rad/s},$ at what rate is its altitude decreasing when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}?$ Assume that the rate of decreasing altitude is **positive** and do not round the answer.

The drone's altitude is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{ft/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/5024a642ac27698d848577165b08e3158d3248d50c064a79432fcad6e2df90d5.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the drone’s altitude, and $x$ is the distance between Ethan and the shadow. The quantity $x=150\,\text{ft}$ does not change with time because the distance between Ethan and the shadow is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{150} \\ y & =150\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(150\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =150{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-0.1$ (negative because the angle is decreasing) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =150{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})(-0.1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =150(4)(-0.1) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-60.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the drone's altitude is decreasing at a rate of $60\,\text{ft/s}.$

A firefighter $F$ is lowering a rescue basket $B$ from a helicopter. The basket stays $40\,\text{ft}$ above the ground while it moves horizontally toward the firefighter at a speed of $12\,\text{ft/s}.$ Find, in radians per second as a function of $\theta ,$ the rate at which the angle $\theta $ between the cable and the horizontal is increasing.

The angle is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/cfac2040d258398133397c5322e650bf60f59c7c372c97bfecec654eb3a4a278.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the basket's height, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the firefighter and the basket. The quantity $y=40$ feet does not change with time because the basket height remains the same.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{40}{x} \\ x & =40\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(40\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-12\,\text{ft/s}$ (negative because the horizontal distance is decreasing). Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =(-40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{12}{40} & =({csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{12}{40}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{10}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{10}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{rad/s}.$
